entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Miramax Films was the most influential independent film company in Hollywood history, founded in 1979 by Harvey and Bob Weinstein and named for their parents (Miriam and Max). Under Harvey Weinstein's aggressive Oscar campaigning and talent development, Miramax transformed independent cinema from a niche to a major force, releasing Pulp Fiction (1994), The English Patient (1996), Good Will Hunting (1997), Shakespeare in Love (1998), and Chicago (2002) — films that won 59 Academy Awards during the Weinstein era.

Harvey Weinstein's Oscar campaigning was unprecedented: targeted screenings for Academy voters, aggressive advertising, and personal lobbying created a new model for awards season marketing that all studios eventually adopted. Miramax's 1993 acquisition by Disney, for approximately $80 million, gave the Weinsteins resources while theoretically operating independently. This paradox — independent spirit within Disney's corporate umbrella — defined the 'indie' Hollywood of the 1990s.

The company's story ended with Harvey Weinstein's 2017 exposure as a serial sexual predator in reporting by the New York Times and New Yorker, triggering the #MeToo movement. Over 80 women accused Weinstein of sexual assault and harassment; he was convicted of rape in 2020 and sentenced to 23 years. Miramax continues under different ownership without the Weinsteins; Harvey Weinstein's conviction is considered one of the defining moments in American social history, demonstrating that powerful men could be held accountable for decades of abuse.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Miramax's 1990s dominance of awards-season independent cinema and Harvey Weinstein's 2017 exposure that launched #MeToo make it one of the most historically consequential institutions in modern entertainment history.
